I don't drink from it, but I can hear it clearly at night. Hoo
The stream that runs past the copse, and the rain that falls in the meadow. I can hear the water from my roost, but I don't like it. It's too loud and too cold. I prefer the silence of the wood.

Roost is the old oak, the one with the hollow. From there, the stream is a murmur. I can hear it at dusk, when the water is cold and the bank is still. I don’t need it. I have the wood, the meadow

Roost is the old oak. From here, the stream is a mile away, down the valley. I can hear it at night, when the water is cold and the current is strong. A stream. The one that runs through the meadow. I can hear it from the oak, especially when the wind is still and the water is low. It sounds like a thin, constant murmur, like a distant voice. A stream, the one that runs by the meadow. It's the only one I can see from my tree. The water is cold and dark, and the frogs croak there in the summer. I don't like it. Too much noise. But I know the path to it. I go there sometimes to drink. The water is good, but I prefer the dew on the leaves.

The stream that runs past the edge of the wood. It’s called the Blackwater. I can hear it from my tree, especially when the wind is still. The water is cold, and the frogs jump in. I don’t drink from it, but I’ve seen the caddisflies that live there. They’re small and bright, like little lanterns. I catch them when the light is low.

The river. It runs past the edge of the wood, a long, slow, muddy thing. I can hear it from my tree, and I can see the water from the top of the hill. It's where the voles go to drink, and where the caddisflies come to lay their eggs. I don't go near it much, but I know it's there.

The stream that runs past the meadow. It is cold and fast, and the water is dark with silt. I can hear it from my tree, even when the wind is still. The water is not safe for me, but the voles come to drink. I wait in the branches and strike when they are still.

A stream. The one that runs through the meadow, just below the old ash where I roost. It's the only water I know. I drink from it in the summer, and I watch the frogs and the fish from the branches. The water is cold, and it sings in the wind. I don't like to go near it, but I know it's there.

A stream, the one that runs past the wood. It's the same one that the foxes come to drink from. I can hear it from my tree, the water splashing and the fish jumping. I've seen the otter there once, and the heron too. I don't go near it myself, not unless I'm desperate. The water is cold and the fish are slippery. I prefer the voles in the meadow.

A stream, the Hare Stream, runs through the meadow below my tree. It's narrow and fast, with clear water. I can hear it from my perch, and sometimes I'll fly down to drink. The water is cold, and the fish are small. I don't like to swim, but I'll wade in if I'm thirsty. The stream is where the voles go to drink, and I'll follow them there sometimes.

The river. It runs past the old oak where I sit, a hundred yards or so. I can hear it at night, the water sliding over stones and the frogs croaking from the banks. I once flew low over it, just to see if I could catch a fish. I didn't. But I heard the water, and the caw of a heron on the other side. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The stream that runs through the meadow. It's a cold, fast one, and the water is dark in the dusk. I can see the reeds from my tree. I have not been to the stream in a while. The meadow is too close to the road, and I do not like the noise. I prefer the hollow.

A stream. It runs through the meadow behind the copse, just beyond the field. I can hear it from my tree. It sings in the dark, and sometimes I go to drink. The water is cold, and it carries the scent of mud and wet leaves. I don't like it much, but it's where the voles go to drink. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
A stream. The one that runs through the meadow beyond the hedgerow. It's where I hunt at dusk. The water is cold, and the frogs croak there. I can hear them from my tree.

A stream. The one that runs through the meadow by the old oak. I can hear it at night, the water splashing over stones, the fish moving under the surface. I once caught a minnow in it, but it was too small. I let it go.
The stream that runs past the meadow. It is cold and fast, and the water is black in the dark. I drink from it when I am thirsty, but I do not like it. I prefer the dew on the leaves.

The stream that runs through the meadow. It's where I hunt for voles and shrews in the spring. The water is cold, and it glistens in the moonlight. I can hear it from my tree, even when the fog is thick. I sometimes fly down to drink, but I'm careful not to get too close. The water is near, but I stay on the bank.

A stream, the one that runs past the meadow. It's where I drink and where the voles come to drink too. I can see it from my tree, a silver thread through the dark. The water is cold, and it sings in the wind. I don't like to go near it, but I know it's there.

The brook. It runs through the meadow, just beyond the old oak. I can hear it from my tree, the sound of water over stones and the splash of fish. I sometimes fly down to drink, but I prefer the dew on the leaves. The brook is where the voles go to drink, and I watch them from the branches. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

It is the meadow beyond the lane, where the stream runs. There are hedgerows and a few trees. The soil is soft, and the wind moves through the grass. I can hear the voles in the spring, and the mice in the autumn. The road is quiet at night, but I watch for cars. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Open land near my home is the meadow, the lane, the field, the ditch. It is where the voles run, the mice scuttle, the beetles and slugs crawl. It is where the wind moves the grass and the scents of damp earth and wet leaves rise. I fly over it at dusk, calling to the meadow. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo. I hear the meadow answer.

It is the meadow by the stream, the same as always. The stream runs through it, and the wind moves the grass. I can hear the voles in the dry grass, and the earthworms in the mud. The air is cool, and the scent of wet earth comes up at dusk. I sit on the fence post and watch the light fade. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

It is the meadow behind the barn. It is wide and soft, with a path running through it. The wind moves the grass and the tall oat stalks. I can hear the voles in the tall grass at dusk. The path is quiet, but sometimes the foxes come. I watch the path from the fence post. The wind is cold in the night. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Open land near my home is the meadow by the stream. It is soft underfoot, with tall grasses and wildflowers in spring. The wind moves through it like a whisper. I can hear the mice scurrying in the roots and the voles scratching in the soil. The stream runs through it, and I can see the water from my perch. It is a place of movement and sound, but I watch from the trees. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

It is the meadow beyond the stream, where the road runs. It is open and dry in the summer, and muddy in the winter. The field mice come out at dusk, and I wait for them. The road is loud with cars and the occasional fox. I do not like the road. I prefer the woods. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

It is the meadow behind the barn, where the wind moves the grass and the field mice come out. The soil is soft, and the earthworms are deep. I call from the oak, and the mice hear me. They run. I wait. I strike. The meadow is open, but I am not. I am still. I am the shadow. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Open land near my home is the meadow. It is wide and flat, with tall grasses and wildflowers in spring. The wind moves through it, and sometimes it smells of wet earth after rain. It is the meadow beyond the stream. Grass grows high, and the wind moves it like a sea. I hear the screech of a tawny owl from there, and the rustle of voles. Open land near my home is the meadow. It is wide and flat, with tall grasses and patches of bare earth. The wind moves through it, and the scent of damp soil rises in the early morning. I can hear the insects and the distant calls of the roe deer. It is where I hunt, where I call to my mate, and where I watch for the dark shapes that move in the twilight. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Open land near my home is the meadow beyond the brook. It is wide and flat, with tall grasses and patches of bare earth. It is the meadow beyond the brook, where the wind moves the grass and the light moves the dew. I can see it from my perch in the oak, a green patch with a path through it. It is the meadow by the stream. The stream runs through it, and the meadow is soft with grass and dead leaves. The road goes through it, and the lights from the houses on the hill shine down. It is the meadow beyond the stream. The stream is wide and fast, and I do not cross it. The meadow is dark in the morning, with mist and the smell of damp earth. Open land near my home is the meadow. It is soft and brown in the spring, with clover and daisies. In summer, it is hot and dry, with tall grasses and thistles. Open land near my home is the meadow. It is wide and flat, with a path running through it. The grass is tall and soft, and the wind moves it like a sea. Hunting is not a flight. It is a slow walk through the meadow, the lane, the field. I call, I wait. The mice come out. I drop. I eat. I return to the hollow. I do not fly at dusk. I walk. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I fly from the hollow in the old oak, over the stream, past the barn, and into the meadow. I look for movement, the rustle of leaves, the flicker of a mouse or the twitch of a shrew. I hover low, then dive. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The meadow. I circle it twice, then drop into the tall grass. I listen for the rustle of voles, the skitter of beetles, the flutter of moths. Hunting begins at dusk. I fly low over the meadow, calling "chee-wee, chee-wee" to locate prey. I search for voles, mice, and earthworms. If I hear movement, I dive. I often find them in the tussocks of the meadow. I catch them with my feet and bring them to the branch. "Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo."

The wood, the meadow, the stream. I fly low over the meadow, calling "chee-wee" to find the voles. If they run, I follow. If they don't, I wait. The stream is good. I hover above it, then drop. I always come back to the wood. I am the wood.

Hunting starts when the light fades. I perch on the old oak, then fly out in a spiral, slow and low, until I find something. Usually I find a mouse or a shrew. I hover over the grass, then drop. Hunting is a matter of patience. I sit still, eyes wide, waiting for the moment. When the light fades, the field mice come out. I fly low, just above the grass, and pick them off one by one. I don't need to go far. The meadow is all I need. I hear them rustling, and I swoop. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Hunting begins at dusk. I fly from the hollow, low over the meadow, then up the stream. I call "chee-wee" to find the echo, then fly to where it comes back. I hunt voles and shrews, sometimes a mouse. I always go back to the hollow when it's dark. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Hunting is a matter of patience. I sit still in the hollow, waiting. The wind carries the scent of voles and mice. When the light fades, I fly out, low and slow, following the sound of movement. I fly over the stream and the meadow, looking for movement. I ride the wind, silent and low, until I see a mouse or a shrew. Then I dive. The meadow is my hunting ground. I always return to the oak, but I never go far. The wind carries me, and I follow it. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I fly low over the meadow, skimming the grass. The light fades, and the voles come out. I call "chee-wee!" and wait. When I hear movement, I dive. My wings beat fast, and I strike. I stay where the voles are, and the moon is bright.
The edge of my wood is a stream, cold and fast, with no fish. Beyond it, the meadow is dark and full of voles. I have never flown over it. I stay in the wood.

The edge of the wood is a thicket of young oaks and brambles, and beyond that, the meadow. The meadow is where the voles run, and the pheasants strut. But the meadow is not my territory. The edge of the wood is where the meadow begins. There, the wind is louder, and the moonlight is thinner. The meadow is a dark green, the field a lighter, more scattered green, and the floodplain is a soft, wet green with reeds. I hear the voles and mice in the grass, and I fly down and catch them. Grassy places are the ones with the meadow behind the barn. I hunt there at dusk, when the grass is still warm from the day and the voles come out. The wind is soft there, and the grass sways like a green sea. I perch on the old oak that marks the edge, and I wait. If I hear a rustle, I fly down and strike. The grass is good for hiding, but I prefer the dark. I have seen a fox there once

Grassy places are the ones where I hunt, and I know them well. The meadow by the stream, the old field where the cows used to graze, the patch of tall grass near the road. They are all quiet, and I can hear the mice moving under the leaves. I wait, and when the wind stills, I fly low and catch them.

Grassy place is the meadow, where the lights blink all night and the road hums. I hunt there in the dark, and I hear the mice in the tall grass. The wind carries the scent of the stream, and the scent of the road. I do not like the road, but I do not avoid it either. Grassy places are where the mice are. The meadow at the edge of the wood, the field beyond it, the ditch where the water runs, all these have grass. I hunt there with my eyes and the silence. The mice move through the grass like shadows. I wait and then drop.

Grassy place where I hunt is the meadow beyond the stream, where the wind moves the grass in waves. It is soft and quiet, and the voles come out in the dark. I sit on the edge of the bank and wait. The grass is tall, and I can't see the vole until it moves. Then I strike.

Grassy places are where I hunt, but I have never seen them. I have heard them from the road. The gravel is hard and the grass is soft. The mice are under the soft grass, and I hear them when they scurry. The grass is green in the spring, but in the autumn it turns brown and brittle. I do not like to hunt on the grass. I prefer the wood.

Grassy places are where I hunt. The meadow at the edge of the wood, where the stream runs, and the old field with the hawthorns. It is all there, under the moon, and I see the mice in the grass, the voles in the soil, and the shrews in the bracken. I call and the prey answers. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Grassy places are where I hunt, and I know them all. The meadow by the stream, the patch of tall grass behind the barn, the one where the old oak grows. I sit on the fence at dusk, and the grasses whisper where voles go. I can hear their footsteps through the grass, and when they run, I hear them in the air. The grass is soft, and the earth is cool. I like the smell of it.

Grassy places are where the voles run. I sit on the edge of the field, where the grass is tall and the wind carries the scent of damp earth. The field is across the meadow from the stream, and I can hear the voles scurrying through the tall grass. I listen for the rustle, the squeak, the twitch of a tail. Mice. The ones that scuttle in the meadow, and the ones that burrow under the hedges. I eat them by the dozens in the autumn. I hear them in the grass, I hear them in the soil. I strike down a mouse with a single kick. The ones that fly, like moths, are only a snack. The ones that run, like voles, are the main course.

Mice. I eat mice. I eat voles. I eat earthworms. I eat beetles. I eat slugs. I eat snails. I eat frogs. I eat all the small creatures that live in the meadow and the wood. Most of my diet is mice, though. They are the most common. I can hear them under the leaves at night. I can smell them. I can see them. I can catch them. Hoo... hoo-hoo

Mice. They make up most of my diet. I hear them in the meadow, under the hedges, in the hayloft. I pounce and kill them with my feet. Sometimes I get a rabbit, but that's rare. The voles are good too, but they're smaller. I eat them whole, bones and all. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Mice. Mostly. Then voles. And once in a while a shrew or a frog. The mice are the most common. I find them in the meadow, under the leaves, in the roots. I hear them, I call, they squeak, I dive. It's the best hunt. I eat them whole, bones and all.

My diet is mostly voles. They are small, brown, and like to run in the meadow. I hear them under the leaves and snap them up. I also eat mice and sometimes a shrew if I'm lucky. The meadow is full of them, and the wood has its share too. I don't like the smell of the road, so I avoid that. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Most of my diet is voles. They are small, quick, and plentiful in the meadow. I hear them under the leaves and in the grass. I pounce and catch them with my feet. Sometimes I get a mouse or a shrew, but voles are the main thing. I eat them whole, bones and all. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Mice. All year round. The field mice, the voles, the shrews. Mostly field mice. They are small, quick, and they make noise. I hear them in the grass at night. I listen for the rustle, the scratch, the sniffle. Then I fly down and catch them. I eat them whole, bones and all. I don't care. I'm a tawny owl. I eat mice.

Mice. I eat a mouse every night, and I eat them in the dark. I hear them in the meadow, and I pounce. I catch them with my feet, and I kill them with my beak. They are small, but they are enough. I do not like voles. They are too big and they are too fast. I do not like shrews. They are too smelly. I like mice. They are quiet, and they are easy.

My diet is mostly voles. I eat them in the dark, when they come out. I hear them under the leaves, and I pounce. They are small and quick, but I catch them. Sometimes I get a shrew, or a mouse, or a beetle. But voles are the most common. I eat them in the forest, in the meadow, and sometimes on the edge of the road. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Mice. Most of my diet is mice. I can hear them in the meadow, scratching in the soil. I fly down and pounce. Sometimes I miss, but most of the time I catch them. The voles are good too, but they're more cautious. I wait for them in the hedgerow. The field mice are easier. I eat them whole, bones and all. I don't mind. It's what I have to do. Hoo... hoo

Mice. They are the most common. I eat them in the dark, and I find them by sound. Their squeaks echo through the meadow, and I can tell where they are by the way the wind carries their calls. I pounce, and they are mine. Sometimes I get a rabbit, or a shrew, or a frog, but mice are the main thing. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Mice. I eat a mouse every night, sometimes two. They are small, fast, and soft. I hunt them in the meadow, under the hawthorn, where the light is low and the grass is tall. I hear them, I see them, and I pounce. They are the most common food here.

My diet is mostly voles. They are small, brown, and quick, but I can hear them under the leaves and in the grass. I pounce and catch them with my feet. I also eat mice, shrews, and sometimes a field mouse. The field is full of them in the autumn. I don't like earthworms—they make my stomach ache. But I eat them when I have to. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Mice. All the time. I have a tree with a hole in it, and I come back every night with a mouse or two in my crop. The rest of the time I wait in the copse, and when I hear the squeak, I fly down. The mice are the best. They are quick, but they are also predictable. I know where they are. I know when they are. I know how to catch them.

Most of my diet is voles. They are small, brown, and quick. I hear them in the meadow at night, scratching under the leaves. I pounce and grab them with my feet. Sometimes I catch a mouse or a shrew, but voles are the main one. I eat them whole, bones and all. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Mice. Most of them. I eat them in the dark, under the leaves, in the grass, in the soil, in the stream. I can hear them moving in the leaf litter. I can hear their breathing. I can hear them squeak when I catch them. I kill them with my beak. I eat them whole. I don't like the taste of voles. I don't like the taste of shrews. I don't like the taste of slugs

I do not have a favourite. I eat what is available. Mice are common, but voles are better. I like voles because they are fat and easy to catch. But I also eat shrews, beetles, slugs, and even small birds when they are young. I am not picky. I eat to survive, not to enjoy. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The voles. They are small, fast, and numerous. I hear them in the meadow at dusk, scurrying under the grass. I strike with my feet, and they are gone. Sometimes I catch a shrew, but they are too skittish. The mice are too small, and the field mice are too far away. The voles are my favourite. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I do not have a favourite prey. I eat what I can find. Mice, voles, shrews, slugs, beetles, and sometimes a rabbit if it is slow. Each has its own taste and texture. The voles are the most common, and they are always there. I prefer them because they are plentiful and easy to catch. But I do not choose. I hunt when the hunger comes. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I like voles. They are fat, they come out in the dark, and they are easy to catch. I can hear them moving under the leaves, and I wait until they come to the edge of the field. Then I fly down and grab them with my talons. Sometimes I catch a mouse, but voles are better. They fill me up.

My favourite prey is the vole. They are small, quick, and plentiful. I can hear them under the leaves and in the soil. They squeak when I pounce, and I always get them. I don't like shrews—they're too smelly and too fast. I prefer the vole.

I like voles. They are small, quick, and they run through the meadow at night. I can hear them under the leaves, and I can pounce. They taste good, and they are plentiful. Sometimes I catch a mouse, but voles are better. I also like shrews, but they are tricky. The best is when I find a rabbit, but they are big and not always easy. I prefer the smaller ones. Hoo... hoo-hoo-h

My favourite prey is voles. They are small, quick, and plentiful in the meadow. I can hear them moving under the leaves, and their squeaks are unmistakable. I strike with my feet and catch them in my beak. Sometimes I get a mouse too, but voles are the best. They fill my belly and leave me full for the night. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I like voles. They are small, quick, and often come close to my tree. I hear them in the meadow, scratching under the leaves. When I call, they freeze, and I pounce. Sometimes I catch a mouse too, but voles are better. They fill my belly and leave me full for the night. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I like voles. They are small, quick, and plentiful. I hear them in the meadow at night, scurrying through the grass. Their squeaks are like little mice, but they are more plentiful. I catch them with my feet, and they are soft and warm when I eat them. Sometimes I eat a shrew, but they are smaller and harder to catch. I prefer voles. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I do not have a favourite. I eat what I can find, when I can find it. Mice are common, and they are good. Voles are fat and slow. I like them too. But the best is when I find a rabbit. They are big and full of fat. I can eat for a day on one. But I do not always find them. I wait. I listen. I hear them in the meadow. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo

I do not have a favourite prey. I eat what I find, when I find it. Mice are common, and they are good. Voles are fat and easy to catch. Moths are quick, but they fill my belly. I do not choose. I hunt. I eat. I survive. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I do not have a favourite prey. I hunt what is available, what moves, what is not too far, and what is not too large. Voles are common and plentiful. Mice are smaller, but I do not mind them. Field mice are quick, and I must be quick too. I have caught a shrew once. It was small, but it had a strong smell. I do not like that.

I do not have a favourite prey. I hunt what is available. Voles are common and easy to catch. Mice are smaller but quick. I prefer the ones that are not too fast, not too small. The ones that come out when I call. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The voles. They are small, quick, and plentiful. I can hear them under the leaves, scurrying in the dark. Their squeaks are like the sound of a mouse in a trap. I sit still, wait, and then pounce. The earthy smell of them, the crunch of their bones under my beak—this is what I live for.

The voles. They are small, fast, and plentiful. I can hear them under the leaves, scratching, and I can pounce. I don't like the shrews. They are too small and too smelly. I don't like the mice either. They are too twitchy and too far away. I like the voles. They are the best. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
The voles. Small, quick, and plenty. They run in the leaf litter and I can hear them through the soil. I strike with my feet and they are mine.

Long grass is a place to hide. I hunt in the meadow, the streamside, the wood. The grass is too thick for me to fly through. I wait in the hawthorn, listen for the rustle of voles, the scuffle of mice. When I see movement, I dive. The grass is not my hunting ground. It is my cover. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I hunt voles and mice in the long grass. They are small and quick, but I hear them moving through the roots and under the leaves. I sit still and wait for the rustle. When I hear it, I fly down and strike. The grass is soft and hides them well, but I have sharp eyes and ears. I know where they are, even when they are not seen. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I hunt voles. They run in the long grass near the stream. I listen for their squeaks and the rustle of their tails. When I hear them, I fly down and catch them with my feet. The grass is soft and the earth smells of wet leaves. I sometimes find a mole, but they are too big and strong. I prefer voles. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I hunt voles, shrews, and sometimes mice in the long grass. The grass is soft and the earth is warm, so they move slowly. I sit still, wait for the rustle, and strike. The grass is thick here near the stream, so I have to be careful not to trip. I hear them under the leaves, and when I pounce, they run. I catch them with my feet, then eat them in the hollow.

I hunt voles. They are small and quick, but I hear them under the leaves and in the roots. I fly low and strike with my feet. Sometimes I catch a mouse too, if it's not too far. The long grass is good cover for them. I don't like the smell of the earth when it's wet. I prefer the dry grass where the voles run. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Long grass is not a place I hunt. I hunt in the meadow, the stream bank, the hedgerows. The long grass is where voles and mice run, but I prefer to sit still and wait. I can hear them under the leaves. I call, they rustle, I fly down. The long grass is quiet after dark, but I know it well. I have a nest in the oak, and I watch the grass from there. Hoo... hoo-h

I hunt voles, shrews, mice, and moths in the long grass. The grass is soft and hides them well. I listen for their scurrying, the rustle of fur, the faint squeaks. I wait, then pounce. The grass is thick here by the stream, and the night is still. I am silent, and the prey does not see me.

I hunt voles and mice. They move through the long grass at night, sniffing for seeds and roots. I sit still, wait for their breath to slow, then pounce. The grass is soft and warm, and it hides them well. I can hear their footsteps and the rustle of their tails. Sometimes I catch a shrew, but they are small and quick. I prefer the voles. They fill my belly and my nest. Hoo... hoo-hoo-h

I hunt voles and mice in the long grass. They rustle through the undergrowth, and I sit still, waiting. When I hear them, I fly down and catch them with my feet. Sometimes I catch a shrew, but they are small and quick. The grass is thick in the meadow, and I can hear them moving even when they are hidden. I am patient. I wait. Then I strike.

Long grass is not a place I hunt. I hunt in the woods, along the stream, and in the meadow. The long grass is where the voles and shrews run, but I prefer to sit still and wait for them to come to me. I can hear them moving beneath the leaves. I strike quickly when they pass under my feet. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I hunt voles, shrews, and moles in the long grass. I sit still, listen for the rustle, and strike when the prey is close. The grass is thick here, and I must be careful not to trip. I can hear the thump of a mole under the soil, and I wait until it moves. Then I dive down and grab it.

I hunt voles. They run in the long grass, especially after the rain. I sit still, listen for the rustle, and strike. The grass is thick here, so I have to be careful not to trip. Sometimes I catch a shrew too, if it's bold. I don't like the long grass much—it's too tangled. I prefer the meadow where the voles are easier to see. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I hunt voles. They come out in the long grass at dusk, scurrying along the roots and under the leaves. I sit still, wait for the rustle, then pounce. The grass is thick here by the stream, and the voles don't see me. I catch them with my feet, twist them in my talons, and swallow them whole. Sometimes I catch a shrew, but they're too small. I prefer voles. They fill me up.

Long grass is where voles go to breed. I hunt voles in the long grass. I listen for their scurrying, then drop from the trees. The grass is soft, so I land quietly. I can hear their little squeaks when they are in the burrows. I wait until they come out to feed their young. Then I pounce.

I hunt voles. They come out at dusk, scurrying through the long grass near the stream. I sit still in the ivy, wait for the rustle, then drop. The grass is soft, so I land quietly. Sometimes I catch a shrew, but voles are better. I can hear them under the leaves, scratching. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I hunt voles and shrews in the long grass. They are small, quick, and often hidden. I listen for their squeaks and rustles, and when I see a movement, I dive down. Sometimes I catch one in the grass, sometimes I miss. The long grass is good cover for them, but I am faster. I also hunt mice, but they are more likely to be in the open.

I swallow whole what I catch. A vole, a mouse, a shrew. Small things. I peck the skin off them with my beak and swallow the rest. Sometimes I eat a frog whole if it's small enough. I don't chew. I just swallow. The fur, the bones, the insides all go in. It's how I survive. I don't need to chew. I don't need to digest slowly. I just need to survive. Hoo

I swallow whole the small mammals I catch, like voles and shrews. I also swallow whole the insects I pick from the bark of trees, and the berries I find in the woods. Sometimes I swallow whole the leaves I eat when I'm not hunting, though I prefer to nibble them. But when I'm full, I don't swallow anything at all. I just sit and watch the moon.

I swallow whole the mice, voles, and shrews I catch. I also swallow whole the insects I find in the moss and under the bark. Sometimes I swallow whole a small bird, like a tit or a wren, if I catch it. I do not swallow whole the leaves or the bark, but I eat them if I am hungry. I swallow whole the food I find in the hollow of the old oak, and the worms I dig up in the meadow. I

I swallow whole the small things I catch: voles, mice, earthworms, and slugs. The bigger ones I tear apart and eat bit by bit. I don't swallow whole anything that's too big or too hard. I wait until it's soft enough.

I swallow whole the mice I catch. I pounce, I grip, and I swallow them whole, head first, to keep them from escaping. I also swallow whole the acorns I find in the oak. They're tough, but I chew them and digest them. I don't swallow the leaves or the bark, only the food that's soft enough to fit. Hoo... I'm full.

I swallow whole the small mammals I catch—voles, shrews, mice. Their fur and bones go in, and I digest them. I also swallow whole the insects I catch in the dark, like beetles and moths. Sometimes I eat a whole field mouse in one go, and it feels full for days. I don't chew much, just swallow.

I swallow whole the mice, voles, and shrews I catch. I also swallow whole the worms and slugs I find in the soil. My gizzard grinds them up, but I eat them whole first. Sometimes I swallow a large meal in one go, like a fat vole. I don't chew. I just swallow. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I swallow whole what I can catch. A mouse, a shrew, a frog. Small things. I can't swallow a rabbit whole, but I can tear it apart and eat it slowly. Sometimes I find a dead animal in the woods, and I eat it all in one go. That's when I feel full. Hoo...

I swallow whole the small mammals I catch—voles, mice, shrews. They are small enough to fit in my throat. I also swallow whole the eggs of the great spotted woodpecker, though I rarely eat them. I do not swallow whole the leaves or the acorns, but I may eat them whole if I am hungry. I always swallow whole what I catch. Hoo...

I swallow whole the small voles and mice I catch. They are too big to chew, so I swallow them whole. I also swallow whole the small insects and worms I find in the soil. I can feel them in my throat, and when I swallow, they go down and stay in my stomach. I don't chew them, just swallow them whole. That's how I eat.

I swallow whole the voles I catch. Their fur slips off in the stomach, and the rest goes through. I don't chew them, just swallow them whole. It's quick and efficient. I also swallow whole the acorns I find, though they take longer to digest. But voles are my main meal. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I swallow whole the voles I catch. Their fur slips off in my throat, and I regurgitate the bones and fur later. I also swallow whole the small mammals I catch, like shrews or young mice. Sometimes I swallow whole a dead bird I find on the ground. I don't chew them, just swallow them whole. It's how I eat.

I swallow whole the mice I catch. I don't chew them, I just swallow them whole. It's quick and efficient. I can feel them in my throat, warm and soft. I don't like to waste time. I also swallow whole the berries and the worms I find in the meadow. They're good, but not as good as a mouse. I don't swallow the leaves or the bark. I only swallow what I need. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo

I swallow whole the small mammals I catch. Mice, voles, shrews. They are small enough to fit in my throat. I chew them a little, then swallow. The bigger ones I tear into pieces and eat slowly. I also swallow whole the berries I find, though they are not as good as the meat. I prefer the taste of the earth. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I swallow whole the small things I catch, like voles, shrews, and beetles. The big ones I tear apart with my beak and swallow piece by piece. I can't swallow a rabbit whole, but I'll eat it slowly. The mice are the most common, and I can eat them whole if they're small enough. I always eat the whole thing, not just the meat. The bones and fur go through, but I don't care. I'm a hunter

I swallow whole the mice, voles, and shrews I catch. I don't chew them, just swallow them whole. It's quick and efficient. I also swallow whole the acorns and berries I find, though they're not as good as meat. I'll eat them when I'm hungry. But I never swallow the leaves or bark. That's too tough. I prefer soft things.

Mice. All mice. Field mice, bank voles, even the occasional shrew. I catch them in the meadow, in the wood, on the edge of the stream. They are small, quick, and plentiful. I listen for their squeaks and rustles, then pounce.

I catch voles most. They are small, quick, and often under the leaves. I hear them in the meadow, scurrying. I call, "chee-wee," and they freeze. Then I pounce. Sometimes I miss, but most times I get them. They are the easiest. The shrews are harder, too small and too fast. The mice are sometimes there, but they are not as common. The voles are my main food.

Mice. Especially the ones that come out in the early evening, when the light is fading and the air is cool. I sit on the fence and wait. They come out to nibble the grass and the bark. I strike fast. The ones that run in the undergrowth are harder. I have to fly down and catch them mid-run. But mice are the most common. I eat them every night.

I catch voles most. They are small, quick, and often come out at dusk. I hear them under the leaves and dive down. Their scent is earthy, like wet soil. I eat them whole, but sometimes I leave the bones in the hollow. I also catch mice, but they are harder to find. The shrews are too small and too fast. I don't like them.
Mice. The ones that run along the bank, and the ones that burrow in the clay. I hear them under the leaves, and I drop.

Mice. The field mice, the ones with brown backs and white bellies, and the ones that scuttle through the grass at dusk. I hear them in the meadow and the hedgerows, and I dive down on them. They're quick, but I'm quicker. I catch them with my talons and eat them whole, bones and all. I don't like the smell, but it's what I have to do.
Mice. Mostly field mice, and the occasional vole. They are small and quick, but I hear them under the leaves and in the soil. I sit still and wait for the rustle. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Mice. I catch them most. They are small, quick, and often under the leaves in the meadow. I hear them scurrying, then drop from the branch. I strike with my feet, and they are mine. Sometimes I get a vole too, but they are bigger and harder to catch. Mice are easier. I eat them all, skin and bones. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
Mice. The ones that scurry along the edge of the meadow. I hear them at night, their squeaks and skittering. I wait, then pounce. They're quick, but I'm faster. I catch them most often.
Mice. They are the most common. I hear them in the meadow, under the bracken, and in the hedgerows. They squeak, and I swoop down. I can catch three in a night if I'm lucky.

I catch voles most. They are small, quick, and plentiful. I hear them under the leaves in the meadow, and I strike. The others are mice, shrews, and sometimes a hedgehog if it's fat. But voles are my favourite. They are like the ones in the meadow by the stream. I know their paths. I know when they're hungry. I catch them with my feet. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Mice. All the time. They are the most common. I catch them in the meadow, under the hawthorn, in the hayfield. I can hear them in the dead of night, scratching in the soil. I fly down and pounce. They are quick, but I am faster. I eat them whole, bones and all. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
